aspects.says: An array's class is fixed when it is created: a String[] is an Object[], an Object[] holding strings is not a String[], and an int[] is not an Object[].
basis: section:Arrays Keep Their Element Type at Run Time; Generic Types Lose Their Type Arguments

aspects.says: A cast lets null through, so a missing value surfaces later, for example as a NullPointerException when it is unboxed.
basis: section:instanceof Asks About the Object's Class at Run Time, and null Has None

aspects.says: At run time a class is its name together with the loader that defined it, so an object of a class reloaded by another loader fails instanceof and the cast.
basis: section:A Class Is Its Name and the Loader That Defined It

aspects.says: javac rejects an instanceof test or a cast that no object could satisfy, judged from the declared types: two unrelated classes, or a final class and an interface it doesn't implement.
basis: section:The Compiler Rejects a Test That Can Never Be True, Judging Only the Declared Types

aspects.says: When a subclass adds state, instanceof in both equals methods breaks symmetry, so a collection's answer depends on which object it holds; getClass() keeps the classes apart.
basis: section:In equals, instanceof Breaks Symmetry With a Subclass, and getClass() Refuses Every Subclass

aspects.says: A generic type keeps no type argument at run time, so an unchecked cast to List<String> checks only List and the ClassCastException comes later, where an item is read; each item must be tested instead.
basis: section:Arrays Keep Their Element Type at Run Time; Generic Types Lose Their Type Arguments

aspects.says: getClass() in equals refuses even a subclass that adds no field; a final value class or composition avoids the choice.
basis: section:In equals, instanceof Breaks Symmetry With a Subclass, and getClass() Refuses Every Subclass
aspects.reason: a design trade-off rather than a right or wrong answer: the practice's ledger requires refusing the subclass, so the cost is discussed on the page, not graded

aspects.says: Java 21 rejects instanceof with a primitive on the left; Java 25 treats it as a preview feature.
basis: section:The Compiler Rejects a Test That Can Never Be True, Judging Only the Declared Types
aspects.reason: the compiler enforces it, so no wrong solution compiles, and the answer differs between the page's Java 21 and the runner's Java 25

aspects.says: instanceof is false for null, whatever the type, because null refers to no object.
basis: section:instanceof Asks About the Object's Class at Run Time, and null Has None

aspects.says: instanceof tests the class of the object at run time, and is true for that class's superclasses and interfaces; Class.isInstance is the same test with the type as a value.
basis: section:instanceof Asks About the Object's Class at Run Time, and null Has None
